subject: Culture
title: Hindu Cremation Rites
description: Learn Hindu Cremation Rites in one minute.

hook.text: At Varanasi's burning ghats, funeral pyres blaze 24 hours a day. The fires have not gone out in 3,000 years.

buildup.text: Hindu tradition holds that fire releases the soul from the body. The eldest son lights the pyre at the head.

discovery.text: The skull must crack during cremation—called 'kapala kriya'—symbolizing the soul's final exit from the body.

twist.text: Electric crematoriums now operate alongside traditional pyres. Families debate whether mechanized fire counts as sacred.

climax.text: Ashes scattered in the Ganges dissolve the boundary between the individual and the cosmic river of existence.

punchline.text: Fire doesn't destroy—it transforms and releases.

quiz.question: What must happen to the skull during Hindu cremation?

details.summary: Hindu cremation is a sacred process where fire releases the soul from the body to continue its journey through samsara. Traditionally performed on an open pyre by the eldest son, who cracks the skull to release the life force, it is one of humanity's most ancient continuous funeral traditions.
details.whyItMatters: Hindu cremation has been practiced continuously for over 3,000 years. Understanding it reveals how one billion people conceptualize death, the soul, and the transition between lives.
takeaways: The eldest son traditionally lights the cremation pyre
Fire is believed to release the soul from the physical body
Ashes are scattered in a sacred river, ideally the Ganges

faq.question: Why must the eldest son light the pyre?
faq.answer: In Hindu tradition, the eldest son performing the cremation rites (antyesti) ensures the father's soul can successfully transition. This obligation is so strong that having a son was historically considered essential for spiritual salvation.

faq.question: Why are ashes scattered in the Ganges?
faq.answer: The Ganges River is considered the goddess Ganga incarnate, with the power to purify and liberate souls. Scattering ashes in her waters helps the deceased achieve moksha (liberation from rebirth).
